about: States for Date Flow's 'Empires & states' axis (doc 18 item 2a): states that have ended and that existing events belong to but the db lacks. Modern states that still exist (United States, United Kingdom, France, India, China...) are left for Ram's decision on ongoing spans.

spans.name: Third Dynasty of Ur
spans.date_display: c. 2112–2004 BCE (the middle chronology; other chronologies shift it by decades)
spans.description: The last Sumerian state to rule Mesopotamia, governed from the city of Ur. Its kings built the great ziggurat of Ur and ran a large, record-keeping bureaucracy, until Elamite invaders sacked the city.
spans.significance: Its law code of Ur-Nammu is the oldest surviving one, centuries before Hammurabi's, and its tens of thousands of clay tablets make it one of the best-documented states of the ancient world.
spans.note: Bronze Age Mesopotamian dates depend on the chronology used; this follows the middle chronology, like Hammurabi's dates elsewhere in the db.

spans.name: First Dynasty of Babylon
spans.description: The Amorite kings who made Babylon a great power. Its sixth king, Hammurabi, united most of Mesopotamia; the dynasty ended when the Hittites sacked Babylon.
spans.significance: It made Babylon the political and religious centre of Mesopotamia for the next thousand years, and Hammurabi's law code became the most famous of the ancient Near East.
spans.note: Also called the Old Babylonian Empire. Middle chronology, as for the Code of Hammurabi.

spans.name: Neo-Babylonian Empire
spans.description: The last empire ruled by native Mesopotamian kings. After helping to destroy Assyria, its kings ruled from Babylon over the Fertile Crescent, until the Persian king Cyrus the Great took the city.
spans.significance: Under Nebuchadnezzar II it rebuilt Babylon on a grand scale and destroyed Jerusalem and its temple, beginning the Babylonian exile that shaped Judaism and the Hebrew Bible.

spans.name: Carthage
spans.date_display: traditionally founded 814 BCE; destroyed by Rome in 146 BCE
spans.description: A city in present-day Tunisia, founded by Phoenician settlers from Tyre, that grew into the leading sea power of the western Mediterranean, with territory in North Africa, Spain, Sardinia and Sicily. It fought three wars with Rome and was destroyed in the last.
spans.significance: Its long struggle with Rome, including Hannibal's march over the Alps, decided that Rome rather than Carthage would rule the Mediterranean world.
spans.note: The founding date is a tradition from Greek and Roman writers; archaeology finds the city by the late 9th or 8th century BCE. It was a colony of Tyre at first and independent later.

spans.name: Classical Athens
spans.date_display: 508/507 BCE (Cleisthenes' reforms) to 322 BCE (Macedon ends the democracy); the city-state itself is much older
spans.description: The Greek city-state of Athens in the age of its democracy, when citizens voted on laws and war in their own assembly. It led the Greek resistance to Persia, built an empire of allied cities and the Parthenon, and lost the Peloponnesian War to Sparta.
spans.significance: Its democracy, drama, history writing and philosophy (Socrates, Plato, Aristotle) became founding models for Western politics and thought.
spans.note: A city-state rather than an empire; the span covers the democratic era, which is when the db's Athenian events fall.

spans.name: Kingdom of Macedon
spans.date_display: traditionally founded c. 808 BCE; Rome abolished the kingdom in 168 BCE
spans.description: An ancient kingdom in northern Greece. Philip II made it the master of Greece, and his son Alexander conquered the Persian Empire as far as India; after Alexander's death his generals divided the conquests, and Macedon itself was later conquered by Rome.
spans.significance: Alexander's conquests spread Greek language and culture from Egypt to Afghanistan, beginning the Hellenistic age.
spans.note: Alexander's events are tied here: he ruled as king of Macedon. The founding date is traditional.

spans.name: Ptolemaic Kingdom
spans.description: The Greek-speaking kingdom that ruled Egypt after Alexander the Great, founded by his general Ptolemy and ruled from Alexandria by his descendants. Its last ruler was Cleopatra VII, after whose death Egypt became a Roman province.
spans.significance: Its kings made Alexandria, with its Library and Museum, the leading centre of learning in the Mediterranean, where scholars such as Euclid and Eratosthenes worked.

spans.name: Qin Dynasty
spans.description: The first dynasty to rule a unified China, founded when the state of Qin conquered its rivals and its king took the new title of emperor, Qin Shi Huang. It standardised writing, coins, weights and laws, and collapsed in revolt soon after his death.
spans.significance: Though it lasted only fifteen years, it created the idea and the institutions of a single Chinese empire, which the Han and later dynasties kept; the name China may come from Qin.

spans.name: Rashidun Caliphate
spans.description: The state ruled by the first four caliphs after the death of Muhammad: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali. In three decades its armies took Syria, Egypt, Iraq and Persia from the Byzantine and Sasanian empires.
spans.significance: Its conquests carried Islam and Arabic far beyond Arabia, and the disputes over who should lead it, ending in civil war, led to the division between Sunni and Shia Muslims.

spans.name: Ghaznavid Empire
spans.description: A Turkic dynasty ruling from Ghazni in present-day Afghanistan. Its greatest ruler, Mahmud of Ghazni, raided deep into northern India and ruled from eastern Iran to the Punjab; it was later squeezed out by the Seljuks and the Ghurids.
spans.significance: Its raids and its rule over the Punjab opened the way for later Muslim states in India, and its court patronised Persian literature, including Ferdowsi's Shahnameh and the scholar al-Biruni.

spans.name: Kingdom of England
spans.description: The kingdom formed when Æthelstan united the English, ruled after 1066 by Norman and later dynasties. Apart from a republic between the Civil War and the Restoration, it was a monarchy throughout, sharing a king with Scotland from 1603 and merging with it to form Great Britain.
spans.significance: Its Parliament, common law and the limits it placed on royal power, from Magna Carta to the Glorious Revolution, became models for constitutional government in Britain, America and beyond.

spans.name: Kingdom of Great Britain
spans.description: The state created when England and Scotland united under one Parliament. It became a leading naval and trading power, began the Industrial Revolution and lost its American colonies, before union with Ireland made it the United Kingdom.
spans.significance: In less than a century it went from a new union to the centre of a world empire and the first industrial economy.

spans.name: Kingdom of France
spans.date_display: from 987 (Hugh Capet); some date it from West Francia, 843; the monarchy was abolished in 1792
spans.description: The French monarchy from the Capetian kings to the Revolution. Its kings slowly gathered a patchwork of lordships into one realm, won the Hundred Years' War against England and, under Louis XIV, became the strongest power in Europe.
spans.significance: Its absolute monarchy became a model for European courts, and the crisis of its finances and authority set off the French Revolution.

spans.name: French First Republic
spans.description: The republic declared when the Revolution abolished the monarchy. It executed the king, went through the Terror, fought most of Europe and ended when its First Consul, Napoleon Bonaparte, made himself emperor.
spans.significance: It was the first large European state to abolish its monarchy, and its ideas of citizenship and rights spread across Europe with its armies.

spans.name: First French Empire
spans.description: Napoleon's empire, which at its height ruled or controlled most of continental Europe. Defeated in Russia and Germany, Napoleon abdicated in 1814, returned for a hundred days, and was finally beaten at Waterloo.
spans.significance: Its conquests spread the Napoleonic Code and ended the Holy Roman Empire, redrawing the map of Europe and stirring the nationalism that shaped the next century.
spans.note: 1804 to 1815 includes the Hundred Days; some end it at the first abdication, 1814 (both years are in the description).

spans.name: Timurid Empire
spans.description: The empire founded by the Turco-Mongol conqueror Timur (Tamerlane), whose campaigns from Samarkand devastated cities from Delhi to Damascus. His descendants held a shrinking realm in Central Asia and Iran until the Uzbeks took Herat.
spans.significance: Its courts at Samarkand and Herat led a flowering of Persian art, architecture and science, and a Timurid prince, Babur, went on to found the Mughal Empire in India.

spans.name: Portuguese Empire
spans.description: The first global sea empire, begun with the capture of Ceuta in North Africa. Portuguese ships opened the sea route to India and built a chain of trading posts and colonies from Brazil and Africa to Goa, Malacca and Macau.
spans.significance: It linked Europe, Africa, Asia and the Americas by sea, and it began the Atlantic slave trade on a large scale. It was the longest-lived of the modern European colonial empires, ending with the handover of Macau to China.

spans.name: Spanish Empire
spans.date_display: 1492 to 1976 (Western Sahara); most of its American empire was lost by the 1820s and its last major colonies in 1898
spans.description: The colonies ruled by Spain, built on the conquest of the Aztec and Inca empires and reaching from the Americas to the Philippines. Silver from its American mines flowed across the world, and its colonies became independent states in the 19th century.
spans.significance: It spread the Spanish language and Catholicism across the Americas, and its conquests and the diseases they carried devastated Indigenous peoples. Its silver helped create the first truly global trade.

spans.name: Russian Empire
spans.description: The empire proclaimed by Peter the Great and ruled by the tsars until the Russian Revolution. It stretched from the Baltic and Poland across Siberia to the Pacific, and at times into Alaska.
spans.significance: It was the third-largest empire in history, and its collapse in the First World War brought the Bolsheviks to power and created the Soviet Union.

spans.name: Empire of Japan
spans.description: Japan from the Meiji Restoration to its postwar constitution. It industrialised rapidly, defeated China and Russia, and built a colonial empire in Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria; its expansion into China and the Pacific ended in defeat in the Second World War.
spans.significance: It was the first non-Western country to industrialise and become a great power, and its wars and occupations caused immense suffering across East and Southeast Asia.

spans.name: German Empire
spans.description: The united Germany created under Prussian leadership by Otto von Bismarck, with the King of Prussia as its emperor. It became Europe's leading industrial and scientific power and ended when the emperor abdicated at the close of the First World War.
spans.significance: Its rise upset the European balance of power, and its rivalry with Britain, France and Russia helped lead to the First World War.

spans.name: Austria-Hungary
spans.description: The Habsburg monarchy reorganised as two partner states, the Austrian Empire and the Kingdom of Hungary, under one ruler. It held a dozen nationalities in central Europe and broke apart at the end of the First World War.
spans.significance: The assassination of its heir in Sarajevo started the First World War, and its break-up created the nation-states of central Europe.

spans.name: Nazi Germany
spans.description: Germany under Adolf Hitler's Nazi Party, a one-party dictatorship that persecuted its opponents and Jewish citizens, started the Second World War in Europe and occupied most of the continent before its total defeat.
spans.significance: It carried out the Holocaust, the murder of six million Jews and millions of others, and its war of conquest left tens of millions dead and Europe divided for half a century.

links.why: The founding of the city by settlers from Tyre began the state.
Rome razed the city at the end of the Third Punic War and made its land a province.
Ptolemy, already governing Egypt, took the title of king and founded the dynasty.
Conquering the last rival state made the king of Qin the first emperor of a unified China.
Abu Bakr's election as the first caliph after Muhammad's death began the caliphate.
The Act of Union merged England into the new Kingdom of Great Britain.
The union of England and Scotland under one Parliament created Great Britain.
Napoleon's coronation as Emperor of the French replaced the republic with an empire.
Defeat at Waterloo ended Napoleon's return to power, and with it the empire.
The proclamation of the King of Prussia as German Emperor created the empire.
Ceuta was Portugal's first overseas possession, the usual starting point of its empire.
Columbus's voyage for the Spanish crown began Spain's empire in the Americas.
Germany's unconditional surrender ended the Nazi state.
